signals.title: Beam is now available — Reflection
signals.excerpt:
# Beam is now available

October 16, 2026| 6 min read

Beam is our first open-weight model, built for advanced coding, reasoning, and long-horizon agentic workloads with frontier reasoning efficiency. Today, we have released Beam’s model weights on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. Our model card includes final benchmarks, and the Beam Safety Technical Report shares the model’s complete safety methodology and evaluations.

In addition to releasing Beam’s weights and documentation, we’re launching with an ecosystem of over 40 partners and integrations to create what we are calling an open operating system for agents. The model is the kernel, and everything above the infrastructure layer is open: reference agentic integrations, deployment containers, inference integrations, and customization pipelines.

Developers can download and self-host the model, evaluate it, customize it for their own domains, connect it to agentic systems, and access it through Reflection and our partners.

...

## Partnering to create the open operating system for agents 

Our vision is to build an open intelligence stack that gives developers, enterprises, and governments control over how AI is deployed in their environments. A model is only one layer of a working system; making it useful takes more than releasing weights. It also requires reliable inference, evaluation, safety tooling, customization workflows, agent runtimes, and deployment paths.

We have worked with partners across the open ecosystem to support inference, quantization, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, agent harnesses, evaluation, and observability. Partners are making Beam available through managed endpoints, cloud platforms, on-premises systems, and sovereign infrastructure.

We are building and releasing our own open-source tools while collaborating with the projects developers already use. Together, these efforts expand a single model release into a usable system with many paths to adoption.

...

Beam has native, day-zero support across the ecosystem including: Transformers (Hugging Face), vLLM (Inferact), SGLang (RadixArk), Unsloth, Axolotl, TokenSpeed (LightSeek Foundation), and Dynamo (NVIDIA) so you can go from weights to a production-scale endpoint without writing custom plumbing.

...

## Agentic development with Mirror CLI

Beam and Mirror CLI are both open-source friendly. We trained Beam along with the Mirror CLI harness to offer best performance, while also integrating with other popular open source harnesses to give developers optionality.

Mirror lets developers run Beam from a terminal, point it at different checkpoints or endpoints, and use it as a daily coding and agent harness. Developers can inspect the agent’s activity, approve tool calls, and steer it as it works. Mirror supports resumable conversations and parallel agents in separate worktrees, while project instructions, skills, MCP connections, and Python extensions let developers adapt it to their workflows.

Mirror’s architecture reflects this design. A Python frontend handles the product layer: prompts, skills, and developer tooling. It talks to a Rust agent core over a local connection, and that core is what actually drives the model. Keeping the core minimal lets it double as a clean evaluation surface, so results produced through Mirror are reliable.

...

Beam has also been tested with Pi (Earendil), OpenCode (Anomaly), and Hermes (Nous Research) across coding and knowledge work, including tasks that involve reading repositories, editing files, and running commands.

All of these harnesses work with Beam today through Reflection’s first-party API, other hosted third-party inference providers, or by self-hosting the model. We’ll keep adding harness support over time.

signals.title: Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM

October 15, 2026 9 min read

Table of Contents

Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM

 We're excited to have worked with Meta Superintelligence Labs to bring Muse Spark Open to vLLM on day 0. Muse Spark Open is an open-weight sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, built for long-horizon agentic coding workflows. It is the most capable US open-weights model to date and it is the model Muse Glimmer 30B was distilled from.

## Highlights

- Architecture: 816B total parameters, 42B active per token with a 1M context window.
- Quantization: Meta released the model in both BF16 and NVFP4. MXFP4 weights were released by AMD.
- Multimodal: Native image and video perception through the same Perception Encoder as Muse Glimmer, with additional audio support.
- Parallelism: Tensor Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism on both Nvidia and AMD. EP, TEP, DEP and PD disaggregation on Nvidia. Initial support on TPU is also available.
- Speculative decoding: We have trained a DSpark draft model, supported on both CUDA and ROCm that accelerates the model performance, tested on the SPEED bench.

...

### Nvidia

Nvidia team improved Muse Spark Open inference across FlashInfer and vLLM through fused normalization, gating, and residual kernels; fused MoE finalization with tensor-parallel communication and RMSNorm; a new low-latency BF16 GEMM implementation and reduced compilation overhead; TEP pooler/unpooler sharding with fused MNNVL collectives; TF32 router GEMM fed by the norm's FP32 output; and improvements to data movement, hardware support, and runtime reliability.

### AMD

Thanks to the AMD team, we have also supported the model on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, in both FP8 and MXFP4 quantized formats, providing improved inference performance and deployment efficiency. Note that ROCm currently supports both Tensor-Parallel and Pipeline-Parallelism.

### TPU

We have added support for Muse Spark Open on TPU on top of TorchTPU. Please contact us or Google for code access. We have also built megakernels for Muse Spark Open. With DSpark speculative decoding (acceptance length = 6), they reach over 650 tokens/sec on 4 TPU v7 chips and over 960 tokens/sec on 8 chips. Without speculative decoding, they still deliver over 270 and 350 tokens/sec, respectively.

...

## Reinforcement learning in vLLM

vLLM also supports LoRA RL on Muse Spark Open from day 0, serving as the rollout engine with Verl FSDP2 as the trainer. vLLM serves the original NVFP4 checkpoint with the LoRA adapter applied on top. The trainer runs on a BF16 dequantization of the same weights and updates only the adapter (rank 32, alpha 64), which covers attention, the MoE latent projections and all routed experts. It also replays the rollout’s MoE routing (R3), and only the adapter is synced back to vLLM after each step.

signals.title: Introducing FastFlow SDK
signals.excerpt:
Introducing FastFlow SDK

# Introducing FastFlow-SDK: Run, Customize, and Optimize Local AI

 Oct 15, 2026

Say you're building an AI application and want local inference running fast: you point your app at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and you're ready. Now, say you need to tune models for a specific workload: you want to customize how they execute. Or say you need closer access to the metal to optimize the operators and kernels, such as GEMM, attention, and RoPE, that make your hardware fast in the first place. Different developers, different starting points, but all of them are trying to do real work on the same hardware.

Here's the catch: most tools only solve for the first case. Point-and-run inference engines get you to a working demo fast, but the moment you need to adapt how a model executes, or build a custom operator, you hit a wall. The serving API simply doesn't expose what's happening underneath it, so you're stuck choosing between an easy on-ramp and real access to the hardware.

FastFlow-SDK removes that tradeoff. It is one-stop platform by AMD for local AI software development, so you can start by running a supported model and keep going as far beneath the surface as your work demands, all within the same eco-system, without switching any licenses, vendors or tool chains.

This first blog in the series introduces FastFlow-SDK and the three technologies that make it possible: FastFlow, IRON, and HRX. The initial release targets Ryzen™ AI NPUs (XDNA2).

FastFlow-SDK meets you on the same stack for whatever advantage you are looking for:

- Run: Point your app at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and get instant speed inference.
- Customize: Adapt model execution and build new capabilities using the tools underneath.
- Optimize: Build and tune operators and kernels directly at close-to-metal level.

...

## FastFlow-SDK

FastFlow-SDK provides a single-entry point for developers targeting Ryzen AI NPUs. It includes support for running state-of-the-art GenAI models while exposing the underlying software stack for developers who need to customize model execution, operators, and kernels.

FastFlow-SDK assembles the following components:

- FastFlow (formerly FastFlowLM) - the application layer for running and serving AI models on the NPU.
- IRON - a close-to-metal Python API for programming Ryzen AI NPUs, built on an open-source MLIR-based compiler toolchain.
- Hip Runtime eXtended (HRX) - a lightweight runtime layer responsible for loading and executing workloads on AMD hardware across Windows and Linux.

...

## FastFlow

FastFlow is an NPU-native inference engine integrated directly into Lemonade, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible streaming API and supports the context lengths of the models it serves. FastFlow also supports tool calling and reasoning models, enabling agentic and multi-step AI workflows on the NPU.

FastFlow supports a range of language, multimodal, speech, and embedding models:

Model Type

Model Families

Text LLMs

Qwen (2.5 / 3 / 3.5 / 3.6-MoE)

Mixture-of-Experts

Gemma 3/4, gpt-oss, Llama 3.1/3.2, Phi, LiquidAI/LFM2

Vision-Language

Gemma 3/4, Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL

Speech

Whisper large-v3-turbo

Embeddings / RAG

EmbeddingGemma 300m

Click here for complete list.

Together, these models provide a starting point for building chat applications, agents, multimodal experiences, speech workflows, and RAG pipelines targeting Ryzen AI NPUs.

...

#### 2. Customize: Build and modify with FastFlow-SDK

Once you're ready to move beyond running models, FastFlow-SDK provides access to the tools used to build and customize them. Developers can experiment with model configurations, integrate new capabilities, and explore how workloads are assembled for the NPU.

As your application requirements evolve, FastFlow-SDK serves as the entry point to the broader development stack and documentation. From there, you can begin working directly with the underlying projects and move deeper into the stack as needed.

To get started, visit the FastFlow-SDK repository for installation instructions, examples, and links to the underlying project documentation.

signals.excerpt:
# Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0

October 16, 2026 11 min read

Table of Contents

TL;DR: Reflection's Beam is a 501B-parameter MoE with 23B active parameters per token. vLLM supports it from day 0 and optimizes it on NVIDIA Blackwell:

- Full feature support. Reasoning, tool calling, and structured outputs work out of the box, and you can run the model with tensor, data, or expert parallelism.
- Agent-driven optimization. Coding agents optimized the model autonomously, making batch-1 decode 2.71× faster and prefill 1.87× faster than our first implementation.
- DFlash2 with adaptive verification. With Beam's DFlash2 drafter, a single request reaches 708 tokens/s on TP8, with an acceptance length of 3.7. Adaptive verification, which decides each step how many draft tokens are worth verifying, adds 10% more throughput at high concurrency.

To try it, use our Docker image `vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam`:

Copy code

```
docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam \
  reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
  -tp 4 \
  --max-num-seqs 128 \
  --reasoning-parser beam \
  --tool-call-parser beam --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER"}' \
  --kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false}' \
  --speculative-config '{
    "method": "dflash",
    "model": "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2",
    "num_speculative_tokens": 7,
    "attention_backend": "FLASH_ATTN"
  }'
```

...

## Agent-driven optimization

Our initial version of implementation was an unoptimized, almost pure PyTorch version of the model. We then optimized it autonomously with coding agents: they profiled the model, wrote the kernels, and benchmarked each change. On TP8, the seven changes below brought batch-1 decode from 8.95 ms to 3.30 ms per step, and an 8 × 2K prefill from 328 ms to 176 ms.

...

## Getting started

The command at the top of this post is a good default: TP4 on a single GB300 node, with DFlash2 and FP8 KV cache. To enable adaptive verification, add `"enable_adaptive_verification": true` to the `--speculative-config`. Other optimizations above are on by default.

- Choosing a parallel setup.

- For the lowest latency, use TP4 or TP8.
- For higher throughput, use data-parallel attention with expert parallelism, e.g. `-dp 4 --enable-expert-parallel`.
- Reasoning and tool calling. The `beam` parsers read the response template that ships with the checkpoint. By default, vLLM also constrains every response to that template, so tool calls always parse and match each tool's JSON schema. `response_format` and `thinking_token_budget` work as usual. To turn the default constraint off, set `VLLM_BEAM_ALWAYS_CONSTRAIN_OUTPUT=0`.

signals.title: Optimized support for Open NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | Red Hat Developer
signals.excerpt:
# Optimized support for Open NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 

October 15, 2026

 Eldar Kurtić Helen Zhao Charles Hernandez Dipika Sikka 

Red Hat AI is releasing optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) model built for long-running agents. These checkpoints are designed to double inference throughput on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs without compromising output accuracy.

These optimizations combine FP8 quantization using LLM Compressor with a DSpark speculative decoding model trained using Speculators, delivering substantial inference performance gains while preserving model quality.

...

## FP8 quantization

To accelerate inference for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, we are releasing an optimized FP8-quantized checkpoint. FP8 quantization reduces the precision of model weights and activations from BF16 to 8-bit floating point, cutting model weight memory and storage requirements in half while preserving model quality.

FP8 quantization is particularly effective on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, which feature native FP8 Tensor Core support and deliver approximately 2× higher theoretical matrix multiplication throughput compared to BF16. Combined with reduced memory bandwidth requirements, this enables higher inference throughput and improved GPU efficiency, especially for large-scale models.

We generated the quantized checkpoints using the LLM Compressor library and its model-free post-training quantization (PTQ) workflow, leveraging the calibration-free nature of FP8 Dynamic quantization.

After evaluating several quantization configurations, we settled on quantizing the attention, expert, and Mamba projection layers of the main model, while keeping the shared experts, routers, normalization layers, and `lm_head` in their original precision. For the multi-token prediction (MTP) layers, we quantized the attention, expert, and shared expert layers, while leaving the normalization layers and `eh_proj` unquantized.

The quantization process is fully reproducible using the creation script provided in the model card.

...

To assess the impact of quantization on model accuracy, particularly in reasoning-intensive tasks and agentic workflows, we evaluate both the BF16 and FP8 models across a broad suite of representative benchmarks. To ensure a fair and consistent comparison, both models are evaluated under identical conditions: non-greedy sampling, four NVIDIA H200 GPUs, vLLM 0.31.0, and the Inspect AI and Harbor evaluation frameworks. The evaluation results are presented in Figure 1. The FP8 checkpoint consistently preserves model accuracy across all evaluated benchmarks.

...

Each upgrade delivers meaningful gains on its own, and they compose cleanly. Swapping MTP for our trained DSpark speculator at BF16 primarily boosts single-user streaming speed, while swapping the BF16 checkpoint for FP8 primarily boosts aggregate throughput under load, where its reduced compute and memory footprint matters most. Combining them outperforms either intermediate configuration at every concurrency level on both workloads.

...

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL models are available for inference through Red Hat Inference Hub on Red Hat AI Factory with NVIDIA.

signals.excerpt:
# Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale 

Published October 16, 2026 

ben burtenshaw

burtenshaw 

Pedro Cuenca

pcuenq 

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

...

TL;DR

> - 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token.
> - Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens.
> - Checkpoint formats: BF16, FP8, and NVFP4
> - Reasoning that can stay in context across turns (`preserve_thinking`), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max".
> - Response template in the tokenizer.
> - Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2
> - Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles.
> - Ships with a Rust-based custom harness.
> - Apache 2.0.

...

## What is Beam? 

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a

...

## Inference Support 

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

### Transformers 

Install the latest version of transformers.

```sh
pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1"

```

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

```py
from transformers import pipeline

pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation", model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B", device_map="auto"
)

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about Python exceptions."}
]
output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens=2000)
output[0]["generated_text"][-1]

```

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

...

### Inference Providers 

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

```py
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://router.huggingface.co/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["HF_TOKEN"],
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
)

print(completion.choices[0].message)

```

...

### Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents? 

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

signals.title: Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model
signals.excerpt:
# Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model

Source: https://pytorch.org/blog/muse-spark-open/

Last updated: 2026-10-15

---

Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse Spark Open runs optimized on the SGLang and vLLM inference engines, with optimization for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel.

Building on our August release of Muse Spark, this open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. The result is a model that is a top open source choice for safety. Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and shares the same base model as Muse Spark 1.3.

...

## Why Helion kernels?

Helion is a PyTorch native kernel authoring language designed for writing high-performance kernels across heterogeneous hardware platforms. Following early adoption from the open-source ecosystem, Helion became a part of the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026. Muse Spark Open ships with Helion implementations of operations such as RoPE, RMSNorm, quantization, etc., delivering 1.03 – 3.95x speedups compared to custom kernels written in hardware specific languages (e.g. NVIDIA CUDA and CuTe DSL) on NVIDIA GB300. These same kernels were directly portable for AMD, scoring similar performance improvements on AMD Mi350 with an overall 3% improvement in end-to-end throughput.

In addition, we also launched Helion megakernels for Muse Spark Open in SGLang. Written entirely in Helion, these kernels fuse multiple operations into a single persistent kernel to improve low latency inference, and can likewise be autotuned for different shapes and hardware.

Helion kernels can be further autotuned by users for broader hardware platforms and workloads – including different accelerator architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, etc.), quantization formats, tensor shapes, and parallelism strategies – without maintaining separate hand-tuned implementations for every configuration. Together, these capabilities make it easier to achieve portable performance while reducing the cost of developing and maintaining specialized kernels.

signals.title: Scale Agentic Coding Workflows with Meta’s Muse Spark Open on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72
signals.excerpt:
Meta launches Muse Spark Open, a coding-optimized 816B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 42B active parameters and a 1M token context window. Trained on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Blackwell Ultra specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. The 1M token context window holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking a task into pieces.

...

## Custom-built for agentic coding multimodal understanding across text, image, video, and audio 

General coding models are optimized for single-shot completions such as generating a function, writing a unit test, or suggesting an inline fix. They excel at discrete, well-scoped tasks where the context is small, and the answer is immediate. Agentic coding demands something fundamentally different. Planning a multifile refactor, navigating thousands of files, recovering from failing tests, and coordinating subagents over long horizons requires a model built for sustained, multistep work. 

Muse Spark Open is built for exactly these workloads, delivering higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. It plans, acts, observes, and self corrects. It supports multistep task execution with tool use, output evaluation, and iterative refinement. The model uses goal conditioning to hold direction and context compaction to retain the knowledge needed to sustain progress across long-running sessions. With a 1M token context window, it holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking tasks into pieces. 

Beyond coding, it searches the web (including multimodal browsing), spawns and coordinates subagents for decomposable tasks, and leverages computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser. It generates separate commentary before each action, so developers know what the agent is doing and why.

...

## Flexible deployment options for Muse Spark Open 

NVIDIA supports multiple inference stacks to meet a variety of developer needs. SGLang, vLLM, and TensorRT LLM give developers direct control over serving configuration, parallelism, and batching on the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform. TensorRT LLM adds compiled engines tuned for NVIDIA GPUs. NVIDIA Dynamo publishes deployment recipes for all three, and separates prefill from decode across dedicated GPU pools, so compute bound prompt processing doesn’t slow token generation. Its KV cache-aware routing sends each request to the worker already holding the relevant prefix, avoiding precomputation as context accumulates across long agentic sessions.

signals.title: Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly

October 16, 2026 12 min read

Benjamin Chislett (NVIDIA)

Table of Contents

Kimi K3 decode performance on NVIDIA GB300.

Coding agents can now help with some of the hardest parts of model optimization: writing complex GPU kernels, performing cross-operator fusions, overlapping computation with communication, and tuning execution across different batch sizes and GPU configurations. For Kimi K3, we used agent-assisted development to build a unified CuTe DSL decode path on the NVIDIA GB300, covering attention, MoE, and communication across 8 or 16 GPUs. The optimizations deliver over 840 tokens/s at batch 1 on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with DSpark (synthetic AL=6), 1.5–2× higher decode throughput in several tested configurations, and up to 1.8× higher P90 interactivity on the AgentX workload.

...

This contribution introduces a new decode path for Kimi K3 which fuses and replaces almost all operations with customized CuTe DSL kernels, tuned for certain subproblems. It targets NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with 8 or 16 GPUs, decode batches from 1 to 64, and optional decode context parallelism for long contexts. The GPUs share one NVLink domain with multicast support. For more details, please refer to the PR.

Kimi K3 kernel timeline: stock vLLM uses 130 microseconds and 23 kernels per layer; specialized decode uses 69 microseconds and 13 kernels.

...

### Decode performance with DSpark

With DSpark, Kimi K3 reaches 842 tokens per second on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs in the controlled AL=6 benchmark. That is 1.73× faster than stock vLLM with the same speculative decoding setup. Refer to the PR for a full results table.

Kimi K3 at batch 1 with TP16, DSpark DL7, and synthetic AL=6: 842 decode tokens/s versus 488 for stock vLLM, a 1.73x speedup.

Setup: TP16, DSpark with seven draft tokens, synthetic acceptance length of 6, DL=7, ISL=1, OSL=1k, batch size 1. TPS measures aggregate decode throughput and excludes prefill.

### Decode performance without speculation

The improvements span across the tested batch range. TP16 retains a 1.62–1.71× gain at batches 16–64, while TP8 delivers 1.31–1.43× over the same range.

| Batch size | TP8 tokens/s | TP8 speedup | TP16 tokens/s | TP16 speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 193.3 | 1.58× | 256.4 | 1.88× |
| 2 | 317.8 | 1.50× | 436.7 | 1.92× |
| 4 | 540.6 | 1.55× | 702.5 | 1.81× |
| 8 | 820.1 | 1.45× | 1,157.9 | 1.79× |
| 16 | 1,274.8 | 1.43× | 1,758.3 | 1.71× |
| 32 | 1,702.6 | 1.33× | 2,550.9 | 1.64× |
| 64 | 2,375.9 | 1.31× | 3,606.1 | 1.62× |

No speculative decoding. Throughput is for the entire TP group.
